name: Diego Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in overpayments and appeals at the Saltmouth regional benefits centre, a grey block by the ferry terminal. When someone's been paid too much, I work out how much, set up a repayment plan, and if they appeal I put the case bundle together for the tribunal. It's a lot of spreadsheets and phone calls with people who are angry, and fair enough. The part I like is finding a mistake that was ours, not theirs, and wiping the debt.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does life look like outside the centre?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a studio flat above a chip shop, so everything I own smells faintly of vinegar. Since my dad had a stroke last year I send my mum a hundred a month, which is why my savings are about two weeks of rent. Most jobs here are at the port or in this building. My mate Kwame left the centre two years ago to train as an electrician, and he keeps telling me to follow him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, some time saved on spreadsheets, nothing to panic about. I'd probably joke at lunch that the robots aren't coming for the overpayments team after all. Most people would shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's safe in that picture, but my money still isn't. The hundred to my mum isn't going anywhere, and the studio rent went up in September. I'm one broken boiler away from a credit card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on in overpayments and keep using the AI summary tool for big appeal bundles, the way I do now and then. I'd look for overtime on the Saturday appeals shifts to build up a month's cushion. And I'd keep Kwame's number handy, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but with a tight chest whenever a bill comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How often do you use the summary tool, and for what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe twice a week, when an appeal bundle is two hundred pages. It pulls out the dates and amounts, and I check them against the payment records. I started using it after half the team did, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one broken boiler away. What happens then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The landlord's meant to fix it, but he's slow, so I'd buy a heater and freeze in the meantime. If it was the laptop or my phone, that'd go on the card. I hate owing money, which is funny given that I chase overpayments all day.

say: I'd say it's **nothing to panic about**, just some time saved on spreadsheets.
I'd joke that the robots **aren't coming** for the overpayments team after all.
think: My **job is safe**, but my money still isn't.
Sending **a hundred a month** to my mum leaves me one boiler away from debt.
do: **Keep** using the AI summary tool on big appeal bundles.
**Take** Saturday appeals **overtime** to build a month's cushion.
**Keep** his electrician friend's offer in mind, just in case.
feel: **Steady** at work, but **tight-chested** when bills arrive.
S0.quote: I hate owing money, which is funny given that I chase overpayments all day.
fieldNote: His pressure is **family duty**: money for his mother after his father's stroke.
He adopted AI **after colleagues did**, typical of his caution.
His friend's **electrician** route sits in the background.

steps.text: Keep using the AI summary tool on long appeal bundles
Take Saturday appeals overtime to build a month's cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a mixed bag. Faster appeals would help claimants, but the centre needs to be honest with staff about which jobs are going. I'd say that at the team meeting, calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Overpayment maths and putting bundles together is exactly what the card means by checking and planning. If the system does the first pass, the team of fifteen becomes maybe eight. I'm average, so it's a coin toss whether I'm one of the eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good with the tools, since that's the safest bet in the short term. And I'd ring Kwame and ask what the electrician apprenticeship actually pays in the first year. If the centre offered voluntary redundancy with a decent payout, I might take it and go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but kind of awake. Like I've been told to decide something I've been avoiding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Kwame say when he left?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He said, 'Nobody's going to automate crawling through a loft with a cable.' I laughed at him then. My friend Kwame left the benefits centre to train as an electrician, and now he earns more than me and never sits in restructuring meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you afford a first-year apprentice wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Barely. First year pays less than I get now, and the hundred to my mum would have to drop to fifty. That's the conversation I'd dread most, not the training.

say: I'd call it a **mixed bag** that could speed up appeals.
I'd ask the centre to be **honest** about which jobs are going.
think: Overpayment maths is exactly the **checking and planning** the card describes.
It's a **coin toss** whether I'm kept when fifteen becomes eight.
do: **Learn** the office AI tools properly as a short-term bet.
**Ask** his electrician friend about first-year **apprentice pay**.
**Consider** voluntary redundancy if the payout is decent.
feel: **Worried** but **awake**, pushed to decide something he'd avoided.
S1.quote: My friend Kwame left the benefits centre to train as an electrician, and now he earns more than me and never sits in restructuring meetings.
fieldNote: He weighs his **odds** coolly: average worker, half the team going.
His biggest barrier is cutting the **money to his mother**.
A friend's **real example** makes change feel possible for him.

steps.text: Learn the centre's AI tools properly this year
Ask Kwame what a first-year electrician apprentice earns
Take voluntary redundancy if the payout is decent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs a proper safety net, quickly, because no one's ready for this. I don't think it's anyone's fault exactly, but somebody has to pay for the fallout. I'd say that to friends, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and the overpayments team is gone. That's pure thinking work, so it goes on the first date. The only bit of luck is that electricians are hands-on, so they'd have until about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrician apprenticeship as soon as I could get a place, even on lower pay. I'd move out of the studio into a room in Kwame's shared house to cut rent. I'd tell my mum the hundred has to become fifty for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and guilty about my mum. That's the worst bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three years for electricians. Is that enough for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's enough to qualify, just about, if I start straight away. I'd be a newly qualified electrician in 2031, competing with a robot, and hoping people still want a human in their house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell your mum about cutting the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a Sunday, in person, not on the phone. She'd say don't worry, she'll manage. And then I'd worry anyway, because I know what her pension is.

say: I'd say the government needs a **safety net**, fast.
I'd say it's not anyone's **fault exactly**, but someone must pay for the fallout.
think: The **overpayments team** is gone on the first date.
Electricians are **hands-on**, so they'd last until about 2031.
do: **Start** an electrician **apprenticeship** as soon as there's a place.
**Move** into a room in his friend's shared house.
**Cut** the money to his mother from a hundred to fifty.
feel: **Scared** for himself and **guilty** about his mother.
S2.quote: I'd be a newly qualified electrician in 2031, competing with a robot, and hoping people still want a human in their house.
fieldNote: He uses the **robot gap** directly to choose his trade.
His **guilt** about his mother outweighs fear for himself.
He's **not looking for blame**, a pragmatic centre view.

steps.text: Start an electrician apprenticeship as soon as a place opens
Move into a room in Kwame's shared house
Cut the money sent to his mum to fifty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but doable, and the centre should help people retrain while they still have jobs. That's just common sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can qualify as an electrician and get a couple of years of work before the thinking AI lands, and five or so before the robots. That's a much better position. I'd probably leave the centre before it pushed me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the centre for a year and save every penny of overtime. Then I'd start the apprenticeship in 2028, so I'm qualified by 2031. I'd keep sending my mum the full hundred for the first year if I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but it feels like a plan, not a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you pick up new things once others have. Is that a problem here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Normally I'd wait to see how it works for others. Here I've got Kwame as the test case, so I'd follow him instead of being first. That's how I do everything, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss about the centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wiping debts that were our mistake. You ring someone, tell them they don't owe four thousand after all, and the phone goes quiet. I'd miss that feeling more than the job.

say: I'd say five years is **tight but doable**.
I'd say the centre should **help staff retrain** while they still have jobs.
think: I could **qualify** as an electrician before the thinking AI lands.
I'd probably **leave the centre** before it pushed me.
do: **Save** every penny of overtime for a year.
**Keep** sending his mother the full hundred in the first year.
feel: **Nervous**, but with a plan instead of panic.
S3.quote: You ring someone, tell them they don't owe four thousand after all, and the phone goes quiet.
fieldNote: He follows a **test case** rather than going first, true to his steady nature.
What he'd miss is **wiping wrong debts**, the human reward of the job.
Five years lets him **protect his mother's money** for longer.

steps.text: Save every penny of Saturday overtime for a year
Leave the centre before the cuts reach his team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to sort this out without anyone falling through the cracks. Government, employers, unions, everyone should have a plan by then. No excuses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is comfortable, honestly. I could stay a few years, save, do the apprenticeship and be a properly experienced electrician by 2036, with robots not until 2039. It'd still change everything eventually, but not on top of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in overpayments for three years, build a real cushion of three months, then go into the apprenticeship. I'd learn more AI on the job in the meantime, because it'll help in the trade too, with quotes and planning. My mum's hundred stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. A bit uneasy, the way you are about anything ten years off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still go, if the centre seemed fine for years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. Even if the centre looks fine in 2030, I know where it's heading. I'd rather leave the benefits centre on my own terms with savings than wait for the redundancy letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new starter at the centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them it's a good place to learn how people's money really works. Then I'd tell them to have a second plan by thirty. Kwame told me that, and I wish I'd listened earlier.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuses** for anyone falling through the cracks.
I'd expect **government, employers and unions** to have a plan by then.
think: I could be an **experienced electrician** by 2036, before robots in 2039.
The change would come eventually, but **not on top** of me.
do: **Stay** in overpayments three years and build a **three-month cushion**.
**Learn** more AI on the job, useful later for quotes.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a mild unease about the distant future.
S4.quote: I'd rather leave the benefits centre on my own terms with savings than wait for the redundancy letter.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him **leave** on his own terms.
His **mother's hundred** stays in every long timeline.
He'd pass on his friend's advice: a **second plan by thirty**.

steps.text: Stay in overpayments three years and build a three-month cushion
Learn more AI tools on the job for later quoting work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It takes my job before I could finish retraining, and I'd have to cut what I send my mum. What would help is paid apprenticeships for people changing career, at a wage you can live on, not first-year pocket money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people we send money to. Lots of people my age are quietly supporting a parent, so when our jobs go, it's not just us who feels it.

headlineQuote: Lots of people my age are quietly supporting a parent, so when our jobs go, it's not just us who feels it.
portrait: Diego is 27, working **overpayments and appeals** at a port-town benefits centre.
He sends his mother **a hundred a month** after his father's stroke, leaving two weeks of savings.
He uses AI **now and then**, picking it up after colleagues did.
His friend Kwame's **electrician** career is the route he follows in every faster picture.
He moves from **uneasy** in the plateau to **alarmed** with two-year AGI.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, taking his job before he could retrain.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for career changers at a wage people can live on.
